title: Trump Backs H-1B Visas Amid Dispute With Immigration Hardliners
description_short: Trump publicly backed H-1B visas in December 2024 amid a dispute between technology supporters and immigration hardliners.
description_medium: President-elect Donald Trump publicly backed H-1B visas on December 28, 2024, during a dispute between technology supporters and immigration hardliners. Reuters reported that Trump said he was a believer in the program and had used it for his properties. The reporting documents a policy disagreement, not a donor exchange or a specific benefit for donors.
description_long: A public dispute over H-1B visas exposed disagreement among Trump’s supporters in late December 2024. Reuters reported that Elon Musk defended the skilled-worker program online while immigration hardliners urged restrictions, and that President-elect Donald Trump publicly backed the visas on December 28. Trump told the New York Post he was “a believer in H-1B” and had used the program on his properties. CNN described backlash over the pro-visa position among parts of the conservative coalition. Reuters noted that Trump had restricted some foreign-worker visas during his first presidency, contrasting that policy with his late-2024 comments. The reports describe disagreement between technology supporters and immigration restrictionists and Trump’s stated support for H-1B visas. They do not show that he exchanged a policy concession for donations or that a particular donor received a benefit. The public argument concerned skilled-worker immigration policy and competing views within Trump’s political coalition.

title: Trump Signed a 2025 Law Limiting Some IRA Wind and Solar Credits
description_short: The 2025 reconciliation law ended certain IRA wind and solar electricity credits for covered facilities placed in service after Dec. 31, 2027.
description_medium: Public Law 119-21, signed July 4, 2025, amended the Inflation Reduction Act’s clean-electricity production and investment credits. For covered wind and solar facilities, the law ends Sections 45Y and 48E credits for facilities placed in service after December 31, 2027, subject to statutory rules. It did not repeal every IRA clean-energy credit.
description_long: President Trump signed Public Law 119-21 on July 4, 2025. Sections 70512 and 70513 amend the Internal Revenue Code’s clean-electricity production credit under Section 45Y and investment credit under Section 48E. The statute provides that these credits do not apply to covered wind and solar facilities placed in service after December 31, 2027, with separate transition rules concerning when construction begins. Section 45Y is a production credit for qualifying clean electricity; Section 48E is an investment credit. The amendments narrow the period in which covered wind and solar facilities can qualify for those specific credits, subject to the law’s definitions and transition provisions. The law did not repeal every Inflation Reduction Act credit. Project treatment depends on its eligibility and construction timeline. The statute does not quantify the effects on investment, employment, or energy output, and does not establish that battery, electric-vehicle, or other clean-energy incentives were ended.

title: Project 2025 Proposals Affecting LGBTQ+ Rights in Schools
description_short: The NEA describes Project 2025 education proposals; its analysis does not establish an enacted LGBTQ+ content ban or criminal penalties.
description_medium: The National Education Association says Project 2025 proposes rescinding federal school civil-rights protections and dismantling the Department of Education. The NEA and National Women’s Law Center describe potential effects on LGBTQ+ students. These are analyses of a proposed agenda; the cited sources do not establish that the federal government enacted a ban on LGBTQ+ content, created a surveillance system, or criminalized educators’ expression.
description_long: The National Education Association’s analysis of Project 2025 describes proposals to rescind federal civil-rights protections in public schools and dismantle the Department of Education. The NEA argues that these changes would harm LGBTQ+ students, while the National Women’s Law Center discusses the plan’s treatment of LGBTQ+ people. The cited organizations describe a prospective policy agenda and its possible effects. Their analyses do not show that the federal government enacted a ban on LGBTQ+ content in media or schools, created a surveillance system, or criminalized educators’ expression. The supplied sources therefore support an attributed account of education and civil-rights proposals, not a claim that censorship or criminal penalties were implemented. The proposals should be distinguished from executive action, legislation, enforcement, or a court ruling. The available record contains no evidence of such an enacted ban or a prosecution based on LGBTQ+ content.
subcategory: LGBTQ+ Content Prohibition and Expression Criminalization

preserved_fields.title: Federal Ban on LGBTQ+ Content in Media and Schools - Expression Criminalization and Censorship
preserved_fields.description_short: Federal Ban on LGBTQ+ Content in Media and Schools - Expression Criminalization and Censorship
preserved_fields.description_long: Donald Trump implemented comprehensive federal bans on LGBTQ+ content in media and schools by classifying any acknowledgment of LGBTQ+ existence as 'pornography' while criminalizing educators, librarians, and media producers who created content that recognized sexual orientation or gender identity diversity through Project 2025's systematic censorship and expression elimination. The systematic content prohibition represented Trump's transformation of LGBTQ+ acknowledgment from protected speech into criminal activity, requiring teachers and librarians to register as sex offenders for sharing materials that discussed LGBTQ+ topics while eliminating federal funding for any educational institution that maintained inclusive content or programming. The LGBTQ+ censorship included eliminating media coverage, educational materials, library books, and online content that acknowledged LGBTQ+ existence while establishing federal monitoring systems that identified and prosecuted violations of content bans through surveillance and reporting mechanisms that enabled systematic persecution of LGBTQ+ expression. Trump's content criminalization violated First Amendment protections for free speech and expression by treating LGBTQ+ acknowledgment as obscenity while using federal power to eliminate diverse perspectives and inclusive content from public discourse, education, and media representation. The expression ban created what civil rights advocates called 'systematic erasure' of LGBTQ+ Americans through content prohibition that eliminated visibility, representation, and educational resources while forcing LGBTQ+ individuals into invisibility and isolation through comprehensive censorship of their existence and experiences. The LGBTQ+ content elimination represented Project 2025's vision of media and education controlled by heteronormative ideology rather than diverse representation, transforming inclusive content from protected expression into criminal activity while eliminating LGBTQ+ voices and perspectives from public discourse through systematic censorship and expression criminalization.

title: Trump Publicly Opposed Approvals for Wind and Solar Projects
description_short: Trump said on August 20, 2025, that his administration would not approve wind or solar projects; the post alone does not define implementation.
description_medium: On August 20, 2025, Donald Trump posted that the United States would not approve wind or solar energy projects, criticizing projects he said harmed farmland and raised electricity prices. description_long: On August 20, 2025, Donald Trump posted on Truth Social that the United States would not approve wind or solar projects, describing them as harmful to farmland and asserting that states relying on them faced higher electricity costs. Bloomberg reported the post as part of Trump’s public opposition to renewable energy and noted that it followed an Agriculture Department announcement ending support programs for clean energy on productive farmland. The post documents Trump’s stated position. His claims about farmland and electricity costs are attributed to him, rather than presented here as independently established effects. The report does not identify which agencies, permits or projects the statement covered, and it does not describe a directive implementing a blanket prohibition. The statement alone therefore does not establish that all wind or solar approvals stopped. The account describes the public comment and its reported context without treating it as a completed administrative action or asserting a measured effect on energy projects.

title: Interior Revises BLM Methane Waste Prevention Rule (2018)
description_short: Interior finalized a 2018 revision of the BLM rule covering venting, flaring, and leaks from oil and gas operations on federal and tribal lands.
description_medium: On September 18, 2018, the Department of the Interior announced that the Bureau of Land Management had finalized revisions to the 2016 Waste Prevention Rule, also called the Venting and Flaring Rule. Interior said the department found overlap with existing state, tribal, and federal regulations. The final rule was published on September 28, 2018.
description_long: During the Trump administration, the Department of the Interior announced on September 18, 2018, that the Bureau of Land Management had finalized revisions to the 2016 Waste Prevention Rule, also known as the Venting and Flaring Rule. The rule covered venting, flaring, and leaks associated with oil and gas production on federal and tribal lands. Interior said BLM found considerable overlap between the 2016 requirements and existing state, tribal, and federal regulations. The final rule appeared in the Federal Register on September 28, 2018, under the title “Waste Prevention, Production Subject to Royalties, and Resource Conservation; Rescission or Revision of Certain Requirements.” The agency record describes revisions to provisions of the earlier rule. It does not establish environmental effects beyond those stated in the records, and describing the action as a revision avoids implying that the entire 2016 rule was removed. The event was a federal regulatory change announced by Interior while Donald Trump was president.

title: Trump Tells Senate U.S. Will Not Join Arms Trade Treaty
description_short: On April 29, 2019, Trump told the Senate that the United States would not become a party to the Arms Trade Treaty.

These records document the decision and later communication; they do not describe withdrawal from a treaty the United States had ratified.
description_long: On April 29, 2019, President Donald Trump sent the Senate a message stating that he had concluded the United States should not become a party to the Arms Trade Treaty. The UN Treaty Collection records a U.S. communication received on July 18, 2019, saying that the country did not intend to become a party. title: Trump Signed the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act on December 22, 2017
description_short: The 2017 law lowered the corporate tax rate to 21% and included a temporary deduction for qualified business income.
description_medium: Donald Trump signed Public Law 115-97, commonly called the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, on December 22, 2017. The statute changed individual and business tax rules; the Joint Committee on Taxation says it lowered the corporate rate from a graduated 15–35% structure to 21% and temporarily allowed a deduction for qualified business income. JCT’s report provides a distributional comparison with prior law.
description_long: Donald Trump signed the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act on December 22, 2017; the enacted measure is Public Law 115-97. The law changed both individual and business tax rules. In its 2019 distributional analysis, the Joint Committee on Taxation describes the reduction of the corporate income-tax rate from a graduated structure ranging from 15 percent to 35 percent to a flat 21 percent. It also describes a temporary deduction for qualified business income. The JCT report compares the act’s distributional effects with the law in effect before enactment and provides separate analysis of business-tax provisions. The law’s distributional effects depend on the year, measure and estimates used. The statute and JCT report establish the provisions described here but do not alone support the broad characterization that benefits were “skewed” toward corporations and high-income earners. The statute also modified individual income-tax brackets and deductions.
subcategory: National Fiscal Collapse and Economic Destruction

title: Massachusetts Court Permanently Enjoins Federal Proof-of-Citizenship Voter Rules for Plaintiffs
description_short: D. Mass. enjoined named federal defendants from imposing proof-of-citizenship requirements on federal voter forms for the plaintiff states.
description_medium: On June 24, 2026, Judge Denise Casper ruled against key parts of Executive Order 14,248 in a case brought by 19 states. A July 13 final judgment permanently enjoined federal officials from requiring documentary citizenship proof on the federal mail voter-registration form and the military and overseas voter postcard form for the plaintiff states. Defendants filed a notice of appeal on September 9. The ruling is scoped to the plaintiffs and the provisions in the order.
description_long: On June 24, 2026, U.S. District Judge Denise J. Casper ruled for 19 state plaintiffs challenging parts of Executive Order 14,248, issued in March 2025. The states challenged the administration’s authority to impose documentary proof-of-citizenship requirements through executive action. A July 13 final judgment permanently enjoined Election Assistance Commission defendants from implementing Section 2(a) or requiring documentary proof on the federal mail voter-registration form. It also barred the Secretary of Defense from implementing Section 3(d) or changing the federal postcard form for military and overseas voters to require citizenship or state voting-eligibility documents. The injunction applies to the plaintiff states and named defendants. Federal defendants filed a notice of appeal from the final judgment and June summary-judgment ruling on September 9, 2026. The notice begins appellate review; the cited court records do not show its eventual outcome or establish a nationwide rule for every state and voter.
